title: Sky treats an exploit in any protocol sharing SparkLend's codebase as grounds for pre-emptive intervention
content:
A.1.10.4.1.1.1 extends emergency multisig authority to "cases where a vulnerability or exploit is discovered in other protocols using the same codebase as SparkLend, and a timely action can prevent or mitigate the damage." The annotation at A.1.10.4.1.1.1.0.3.1 makes the reference concrete: "same codebase" means SparkLend is based on the Aave codebase, and vulnerabilities in Aave "or any other protocol utilizing the Aave codebase, could potentially be replicated and affect SparkLend."

The non-obvious consequence is a redefinition of what counts as evidence of a threat. Normally an emergency requires something happening to *your* system. Here, a disclosure about a sibling fork is sufficient — the shared codebase converts someone else's incident into your own confirmed vulnerability.

This is code-reuse risk stated as governance policy rather than as engineering folklore. Forking a battle-tested protocol lowers development cost and inherits its audit history, but it also correlates your failure modes with every other fork's. The Atlas's answer is not to avoid the fork but to widen the trigger: monitor the whole codebase family, and treat their exploits as your own countdown.
description: SparkLend is a fork of the Aave codebase, so a vulnerability found in Aave or another Aave fork is treated as latent in SparkLend before it is exploited there.
